references.title: University Physics Volume 1, 15.6 Forced Oscillations
references.retainedContentKind: Reviewer paraphrase and equation identification, not a verbatim page capture.
locations: Definition of natural frequency and external driving frequency
Figure 15.31 textual caption and following bandwidth discussion
supports: Sound waves can force another mechanical sound-producing oscillator.
The frequency to compare with the receiver's natural frequency is the external driving frequency.
For positive linear damping, equation 15.29 gives a finite, continuous amplitude as driving or natural frequency changes.
Lower damping gives a narrower and stronger resonant response, not zero response at every unequal frequency.
references.limitations: Only the displayed differential equation, amplitude formula and qualitative bandwidth discussion are used. Simplified exact-peak claims and the page's inconsistent Q wording are not adopted. No tuning-fork measurement or exact clip mass is supplied.

references.title: Oscillations and Simple Harmonic Motion
references.retainedContentKind: Reviewer paraphrase and equation identification, not a verbatim page capture.
locations: Quantitative Analysis and frequency dependence on mass and stiffness
Resonance: harmonic forcing, steady-state amplitude and finite bandwidth
supports: Free motion and externally forced motion are distinct; damping need not be zero for freely vibrating real apparatus.
The harmonic external-force frequency and the receiver's characteristic frequency are separate parameters.
The forced linear-oscillator amplitude formula corroborates finite-width continuous response.
Changing inertia can change a mode's natural frequency; added clip detuning is physically plausible, but its response magnitude cannot be universal without its effective loading.
Drive amplitude, losses and frequency mismatch affect response, while actual acoustic audibility requires additional apparatus and listening conditions.
references.limitations: No embedded media loaded into model context. Use the displayed amplitude formula and qualitative discussion, not apparent typographic mistakes or the page's inconsistent later Q algebra. No empirical sound threshold is inferred.

analyticalInference.reasoning: For gamma>0 and omegaDrive>0 the denominator remains nonzero near matching frequencies. Therefore arbitrarily small nonzero mismatch cannot imply a greatly reduced amplitude. This is an independent inference from both primary formulas, not a quoted universal claim from a source.
analyticalInference.weakDampingPeakCaveat: The displacement-amplitude peak is at sqrt(omegaNatural^2-2*gamma^2) when positive, approaching the natural frequency for weak damping. 'Near' is appropriate; exact frequency equality is not asserted as a universal maximum.
analyticalInference.scope: Reviewer evidence only. No equation, numeric value, experiment or task was added to the learner candidate.
